name: Space-to-Earth Power Beaming
use: Grid power from orbit, remote and disaster-zone power
what: Collecting solar power in orbit and sending it to the ground as a microwave beam. Caltech's MAPLE experiment beamed power wirelessly in orbit in 2023 and its signal was picked up on Earth — the first in-space demonstration of the principle.
how: Photovoltaic arrays in orbit feed phased-array microwave transmitters; a ground antenna field (rectenna) converts the beam back to electricity. The beam is steered electronically, with no moving parts.

name: Lunar Regolith Construction
what: Building on the Moon with local soil instead of launching materials from Earth — the precondition for any large off-world infrastructure, because launch mass is the dominant cost.
how: Regolith is fused with lasers or microwaves, or bound into a printable concrete-like material, then laid down layer by layer by robotic printers.

name: Kinetic & Electromagnetic Launch
use: Bulk payloads to orbit, exporting lunar material
what: Throwing payloads toward orbit from a ground machine instead of burning rocket fuel. SpinLaunch has flown suborbital test shots from a centrifugal accelerator; electromagnetic mass drivers remain a design concept, most practical on the airless Moon.
how: A centrifuge or a linear electromagnetic track accelerates the payload before release. From Earth the payload must survive thousands of g and atmospheric heating, so a small rocket stage still finishes the climb to orbit.

name: Asteroid Resource Extraction
use: In-space propellant, metals for orbital construction
what: Mining asteroids for water and metals. Water is the near-term prize because it can be split into rocket propellant in space. Only small prospecting spacecraft have flown so far; no material has been mined commercially.
how: Prospecting craft characterise a target; proposed extraction heats or grinds asteroid material to release water and separate metals, processing it where it is found rather than shipping raw rock.

name: Planetary Terraforming
use: Making another planet habitable without pressure suits
what: Deliberately changing a planet's atmosphere and temperature so people could live on its surface. For Mars this means thickening and warming the atmosphere; published studies disagree on whether Mars holds enough carbon dioxide to do it.
how: Proposed routes include releasing greenhouse gases or engineered heat-trapping particles, orbital mirrors, and importing volatiles from comets — every route is measured in centuries.

name: Dyson Swarm
what: A Dyson swarm is a very large number of independently orbiting solar collectors that together intercept a substantial fraction of a star's radiant output and convert it into power, computation or directed radiation. Unlike a solid shell it is assembled incrementally, so a partial swarm delivers returns from the first unit deployed.
how: Collector satellites are manufactured from asteroidal or lunar material, positioned in close solar orbit by light sails or electromagnetic launch, and linked by optical or microwave power beams. Because no single structure spans the star, every element is individually orbit-bound and the swarm scales by replication rather than by one heroic construction project.

name: Star Lifting
what: Star lifting is the extraction of matter from a star's outer layers to extend its main-sequence lifetime, alter its spectrum, or harvest metals and helium for construction. The extracted plasma doubles as reaction mass and as feedstock for megastructure assembly.
how: Proposals use magnetohydrodynamic pumping, in which powerful magnetic fields tap the star's own plasma and guide it toward the poles, or a directed beam that ablates a small region of the photosphere. The lifted material is captured at the poles and separated into hydrogen, helium and trace metals.

name: Lunar Helium-3 Harvesting
what: Helium-3 implanted in lunar regolith by solar wind is proposed as fuel for aneutronic fusion reactions that release charged particles rather than neutrons. Harvesting it means strip mining and heating enormous volumes of regolith, so the economics depend entirely on fusion designs that actually work.
how: Regolith is excavated, heated in a solar furnace to drive off trapped gases, and the evolved helium is separated cryogenically. Concentrations run at a few parts per billion, so throughput and energy input, not chemistry, are the binding constraints.

name: Antimatter Production at Scale
what: Antimatter is the highest energy density propellant and energy store known, but it is produced today only in microscopic quantities at accelerator facilities. A civilisation-scale capability would require dedicated production rings powered by close solar orbit.
how: High-energy protons strike a target to produce antiprotons, which are captured, decelerated and stored in Penning traps inside magnetic bottles. The energy cost of production far exceeds the energy recoverable, so the value lies in specific impulse and storage density rather than in net power.

name: Black Hole Energy Extraction
what: Rotating black holes store extractable rotational energy in their ergosphere, a region where spacetime is dragged around faster than light can orbit. Extraction could in principle power a civilisation from a single stellar-mass black hole for longer than the present age of the universe.
how: In the Penrose process a body or field splits inside the ergosphere so one fragment falls in with negative energy while the other escapes with more energy than the original. The electromagnetic version, the Blandford-Znajek mechanism, harvests the same rotational energy through magnetic field lines threading the horizon and is thought to drive astrophysical jets.

name: Shkadov Thruster
what: A Shkadov thruster is a single-sided mirror held above a star by radiation pressure, reflecting a fraction of the star's light asymmetrically. The resulting imbalance produces a slow thrust capable of moving an entire stellar system over millions of years without consuming fuel.
how: A statite, a mirror supported by radiation pressure rather than orbiting, sits at a fixed point above one stellar pole and is angled to reflect light away from the desired direction of travel. Net acceleration is on the order of metres per second per million years, which is small but cumulative and free.

name: Orbital Ring
what: An orbital ring is a continuous tube or cable encircling a planet, held above the atmosphere by a faster-moving inner core of magnetically levitated mass. Once built it provides cheap, electrically driven access to orbit from any point along the ring.
how: The outer static sheath is supported by the momentum of an inner rotor travelling at orbital velocity, magnetically coupled so the net force is outward. Payloads climb the stationary structure and are accelerated by the rotor's momentum through linear motors.

name: Space Elevator
what: A space elevator is a ribbon anchored at the equator and extending past geostationary altitude, held taut by centrifugal effect and a counterweight beyond synchronous orbit. Climbers then ascend electrically, replacing rocket delta-v with a long climb.
how: The ribbon must survive its own weight, which drives interest in carbon nanotube and boron nitride composites with specific strength far above steel. A climber grips the ribbon and drives upward using photovoltaic-powered rollers or linear induction, with debris and weather damage to the ribbon the dominant risk.

name: O'Neill Cylinder
what: An O'Neill cylinder is a counter-rotating pair of large pressurised cylinders that generate artificial gravity by rotation and enclose a closed agricultural and urban landscape. It is the canonical design for a permanent, self-sufficient habitat off Earth.
how: Rotation of roughly one revolution per minute on a kilometre-scale radius produces about one g at the inner surface. Sunlight enters through external mirrors, and pairing counter-rotating cylinders cancels net angular momentum so the assembly can be aimed without expending reaction mass.

name: Bishop Ring
what: A Bishop Ring is an open-topped rotating habitat hundreds of kilometres in radius, holding in its atmosphere by the tensile strength of its own rim rather than by a closed pressure wall. Its usable surface approaches that of a small world while remaining an artificial structure.
how: Because the rim is open, atmosphere is retained by a wall hundreds of kilometres tall at the edge, and the structure is held together purely by hoop tension in carbon-based material. Gravity varies slightly with altitude, creating a permanent radial gradient that shapes where settlement and agriculture can sit.

name: Topopolis
what: A topopolis is a tube of habitat rotating about its own long axis and wound around a star or star system, producing interior area far exceeding any single ring. It scales by extension rather than by building at a larger radius.
how: Each segment rotates to supply gravity while the tube as a whole orbits, and segments are joined by bearings that permit relative rotation. The concept trades structural tensile limits against the sheer quantity of material required.

name: Alderson Disk
what: An Alderson Disk is a thick circular plate with a star oscillating through its central aperture, giving one face continuous illumination and an enormous habitable surface. It is the largest habitable-area concept that remains gravitationally plausible without exotic matter.
how: The disk is thick enough to supply surface gravity from its own mass and is stabilised by the star passing back and forth through the central hole. Structural strength, not orbital mechanics, is the limiting factor and no known material approaches the requirement.

name: Matrioshka Brain
what: A Matrioshka brain is a nested set of Dyson shells at increasing radii, each layer running computation on the waste heat of the layer beneath it. Its purpose is computation rather than habitation or power export.
how: Each shell operates at a lower temperature than the one inside it, so stellar energy is reused at successively lower exergy until it is finally radiated as infrared. The ceiling is set by the Landauer bound on irreversible computation and by the temperature of the cosmic microwave background.

name: Active Support Structure
what: Active support replaces passive material strength with controlled forces, allowing structures far larger than any material could otherwise hold. Compression members are held by thrown or recirculated mass streams and tension members by rapidly moving cables.
how: A stream of pellets or a loop of cable circulates through a sleeve, deflecting at each end and transferring momentum into the structure, so the member behaves as though it had enormous strength. Control bandwidth must be high enough to damp oscillation, making this a control problem rather than a materials one.

name: Generation Ship
what: A generation ship is a self-contained habitat travelling between stars for centuries, carrying a population that lives and dies aboard and arrives with no living crew who departed Earth. Its hardest design problem is social and ecological closure, not propulsion.
how: Propulsion comes from fusion, antimatter catalysis or beamed sails, while the habitat uses rotating rings for gravity and closed-loop agriculture, waste and atmosphere recycling. Dominant failure modes are genetic drift in a small founding population, loss of technical knowledge, and ecological instability across hundreds of generations.

name: Orbital Propellant Depot
what: A propellant depot is a tanker station in low Earth orbit or at a Lagrange point that stores cryogenic propellant and transfers it to visiting spacecraft. It converts launch capacity into deep-space delta-v without redesigning any single vehicle.
how: Liquid hydrogen, oxygen or methane is stored under multilayer insulation and, for long durations, active cryocooling to limit boil-off. Docking, fluid transfer in microgravity and gauging without settling are the hard parts, and they are being demonstrated on orbit now.

name: Lagrange Point Infrastructure
what: The five Lagrange points are gravitational parking places where a station holds position with minimal stationkeeping, making them the natural sites for depots, telescopes, relay satellites and assembly yards. They are the low-energy hubs of the Earth-Moon and Sun-Earth systems.
how: A body at a Lagrange point co-orbits with the two primaries, and small halo orbits around the unstable points are maintained with periodic burns. Their value comes from accessibility at low delta-v rather than from intrinsic stability.

name: Hollow Asteroid Habitat
what: An asteroid can be excavated and spun up so that its own mass supplies radiation shielding and gravity, avoiding the launch of structural material from Earth. The regolith becomes the habitat shell and the shielding at the same time.
how: The body is mined from the inside, the interior pressurised and sealed, and the asteroid spun so the inner surface experiences centripetal gravity. Spin-up needs either mass drivers throwing excavated rock or a tangential thrust phase, and the shell must be reinforced against the resulting tension.

name: Rotating Skyhook
what: A skyhook is a long rotating tether whose lower tip moves slowly enough at perigee to be caught by a suborbital vehicle, then lifts the payload toward orbital velocity as it swings upward. It multiplies existing launch capability rather than replacing it.
how: The tether rotates end over end while its centre of mass follows an orbit, and tip velocity is matched to the capture vehicle by phasing. Momentum is transferred to the payload on every catch and must be restored by solar-electric propulsion.

name: Launch Loop
what: A launch loop is a moving cable running inside a vacuum tube, supported above the atmosphere by its own momentum, with the tube curving down to ground anchors at both ends. Payloads are accelerated magnetically along the cable and released at altitude with orbital velocity.
how: The cable circulates at several kilometres per second inside a magnetically levitated sheath, so the structure needs no tower and only two small ground anchors. Rotor energy, cable strength and control of a floating structure tens of kilometres high are the binding constraints.

name: Beamed Energy Propulsion
what: Beamed propulsion uses a ground-based or orbital laser or microwave array to push a vehicle or lightsail, so the energy source stays behind and the craft carries no propellant. It is the only near-term route to gram-scale probes at a fraction of light speed.
how: A phased array focuses coherent light onto a reflective sail or a heat-exchanger thrust plate, and the beam is held on target by active tracking. Diffraction sets the maximum useful range for a given aperture, which is why very large ground arrays and extremely thin sails go together.

name: Nuclear Pulse Propulsion
what: Nuclear pulse propulsion detonates small nuclear devices behind a pusher plate to reach velocities no chemical rocket can approach. It remains the highest specific impulse concept that relies only on demonstrated physics and existing materials.
how: A magazine of shaped charges is ejected and detonated at a fixed standoff distance, and the resulting plasma and radiation momentum is absorbed by a massive plate coupled to the vehicle through shock absorbers. Momentum transfer per pulse sets thrust, and the plate rather than the device is the engineering bottleneck.

name: Direct Fusion Drive
what: A direct fusion drive uses a compact fusion reactor that exhausts its own high-velocity plasma as propellant, delivering electrical power and thrust from one machine. It would cut outer solar system transit times from years to months.
how: A field-reversed configuration or similar plasma is heated to fusion conditions and confined magnetically, and the escaping plasma is shaped and expanded by a magnetic nozzle. The result is moderate thrust at very high exhaust velocity, which suits long-duration transfers more than surface launch.

name: Bussard Interstellar Ramjet
what: A ramjet collects interstellar hydrogen with a magnetic or electrostatic scoop and burns it in a fusion reactor, so a vehicle could in principle accelerate indefinitely without carrying fuel. It is the classic answer to the fuel mass problem of interstellar flight.
how: A magnetic field hundreds to thousands of kilometres across funnels ionised hydrogen into a reaction chamber where it is compressed and fused. Scoop drag and the extreme rarefaction of interstellar gas make net acceleration negative at low speed, which is why the idea remains theoretical.

name: In-Situ Resource Utilisation
what: ISRU is the production of propellant, oxygen, water and building material from local planetary or lunar material, so a mission carries machinery rather than consumables. It is the difference between a visit and a sustained presence.
how: Core processes are regolith excavation and heating for oxygen, water ice electrolysis, and Sabatier or Bosch reactions that combine Martian carbon dioxide with hydrogen to make methane and water. Reactor power, not the chemistry, is the dominant mass item.

name: Von Neumann Probe
what: A Von Neumann probe is a self-replicating spacecraft that reaches a star system, mines local material and builds copies of itself, producing exponential growth in coverage. It converts interstellar exploration from a series of missions into a single seeding event.
how: Each seed craft carries a complete industrial and computational capability, including mining, refining, fabrication and propulsion, plus the instructions to build another. The core design problem is closure, since any component that cannot be made from local material must be stockpiled or substituted.

name: Galactic Colonisation Wave
what: The colonisation wave is the aggregate behaviour of settlement spreading through a galaxy at a fraction of light speed once travel is solved, occupying a new star every few hundred to few thousand years. Crossing the galaxy at one per cent of light speed takes on the order of ten million years.
how: Expansion is a population and logistics process rather than a single vehicle, since each settled system sends out further missions when it has surplus capacity. Reaching distance is set by cruise velocity and settlement rate, and the absence of any observed wave is the core of the Fermi paradox.

name: Gravitational Lens Communication
what: A transmitter placed at the solar gravitational focal region, beyond roughly 550 astronomical units, can use the Sun itself as a thousand-kilometre-class lens to send a signal to another star with very low divergence. The same geometry works in reverse for reception.
how: Gravitational bending focuses radiation from a distant source along a line where the Sun acts as an annular lens, and gain rises with the square of the lens diameter. A relay must be held in a precise position, and the enormous distance from Earth is the practical obstacle.

name: Jupiter Brain
what: A Jupiter Brain is computing substrate built from the mass of a gas giant, operating near the physical limits of energy efficiency and cooling. It represents the largest computation a single planetary mass can support without stellar-scale power input.
how: The planet's hydrogen is converted into a dense computational lattice, with waste heat radiated from the surface and computation arranged in three dimensions to keep signal delays short. Cooling rather than fabrication sets the ceiling, because thermal radiation grows only with surface area.

name: Grid-Scale Fusion Power Plant
what: Magnetic and inertial confinement fusion approaches are moving from laboratory gain to engineering power plants, with several private designs targeting net electricity on the grid rather than plasma break-even. High-temperature superconducting magnets are the key enabler for the compact tokamak path.
how: Deuterium-tritium plasma is confined magnetically or compressed inertially until fusion conditions are reached; the neutron flux is absorbed in a blanket that breeds tritium and drives a steam or Brayton cycle.

name: Orbital Data Centre
use: Compute offload, solar-powered inference, heat rejection in vacuum
what: Server racks placed in low Earth orbit receive near-continuous solar power and reject waste heat by radiation rather than water evaporation, avoiding land, water and grid constraints on Earth. Early spacecraft have already flown GPUs and returned results to ground stations.
how: Racks are mounted on a solar-facing bus, with large radiative panels rejecting heat; inter-satellite laser links carry data to ground stations, trading downlink bandwidth against compute localisation.

name: In-Space Manufacturing and Reentry Return
use: Pharmaceutical crystals, fibre optics, alloys returned to Earth
what: Microgravity improves the purity of protein crystals, the uniformity of ZBLAN optical fibre and the homogeneity of certain alloys, and small reentry capsules now return these products intact. This is the first commercially plausible off-world manufacturing loop.
how: A pressurised or unpressurised spacecraft hosts the process during orbit, then deorbits with a heat shield and parachute to deliver product to a recovery zone.

name: Planetary Supergrid Interconnection
use: Moving bulk renewable power across continents and time zones
what: Ultra-high-voltage direct current links spanning thousands of kilometres let desert solar and high-latitude wind serve distant load centres, smoothing the diurnal and seasonal mismatch that no amount of local storage fully solves. Submarine intercontinental links are the limiting engineering case.
how: Converter stations rectify alternating current to high-voltage direct current, transmit over overhead or submarine cable, and invert back at the receiving end, with voltage-source converters providing grid-forming support.

name: Deep-Space Communications Relay Network
use: Continuous telemetry and command for outer-planet and interstellar precursors
what: Large parabolic antenna networks with X-band and Ka-band uplinks, plus optical laser terminals, provide the only link to spacecraft beyond lunar distance. Relay orbiters extend coverage through planetary occultations and enable higher data rates from deep space.
how: Ground stations schedule passes and lock onto spacecraft carriers; deep-space transponders use coherent ranging for navigation, while optical terminals trade narrow beamwidth for gigabit-class return rates.

name: Reusable Super-Heavy Launch Vehicle
use: Bulk payload delivery, tanker flights, crew transport
what: Fully and partially reusable super-heavy boosters have cut the marginal cost per kilogram to low Earth orbit by more than an order of magnitude and made hundred-tonne single-launch payloads routine. Reuse cadence, not payload capacity, is now the binding constraint on orbital infrastructure growth.
how: The booster returns under aerodynamic control and lands propulsively or is caught by a ground structure, while the upper stage performs orbital insertion and either recovers or is expended depending on the architecture.

name: Nuclear Thermal Propulsion
use: Fast transit to Mars, high-thrust deep-space burns
what: Fission reactors heating hydrogen propellant deliver roughly twice the specific impulse of chemical rockets at comparable thrust, halving transit times and reducing crew radiation exposure. Reactor fuel elements that survive high-temperature hydrogen corrosion are the central materials challenge.
how: A reactor core heats hydrogen gas to thousands of kelvin through channels in the fuel elements; the gas expands through a nozzle to produce thrust without combustion.

name: Air-Breathing Hypersonic Spaceplane
use: Aircraft-like access to the upper atmosphere and low orbit
what: Combined-cycle engines running in air-breathing mode up to high Mach numbers before transitioning to rocket mode promise aircraft-like launch operations and rapid point-to-point transit. Thermal management of the airframe and engine inlet remains the pacing problem.
how: A turbine or ramjet accelerates to supersonic combustion conditions, then scramjet operation continues to the air-breathing ceiling before a rocket mode completes ascent.

name: Reusable Upper Stage Recovery
use: Full-stack reusability, orbital return of hardware
what: Recovering the second stage is the final barrier to complete launch reuse, since the upper stage is the largest single expendable cost. Designs range from propulsive return with a heat shield to metallic aeroshells with actively cooled leading edges.
how: The stage reenters nose-first behind a regeneratively cooled heat shield or a metallic aerospike, then performs a propulsive landing burn on the same engines used for orbital insertion.

name: Mass-Produced Small Launch Vehicle
what: Electron-class vehicles using electric-pump or printed engines have turned dedicated smallsat launch into a production-line activity, with carbon-composite tanks and additive-manufactured chambers reducing part count and lead time. Responsive launch cadence matters more than unit cost for defence and constellation replenishment.
how: A small turbopump or electric-pump-fed engine powers a lightweight composite airframe; launch is conducted from fixed or mobile pads with rapid integration.

name: Lunar Fission Surface Power
what: Fission reactors in the tens-of-kilowatts class would operate through the two-week lunar night that defeats solar-plus-battery systems. Qualifying fuelled hardware for launch and landing is the pacing item, not the reactor physics.
how: A compact fast reactor with heat-pipe or Stirling conversion is buried in regolith for shielding, with waste heat rejected by large radiators sized for vacuum operation.

name: Rotating Artificial-Gravity Habitat
what: A rotating structure reproducing lunar or Earth gravity removes the largest medical unknown from multi-year missions. Large radius and low rotation rate are needed together, because a small fast-spinning habitat produces vestibular side effects worse than the weightlessness it replaces.
how: A tether or torus spins about its centre of mass so that centripetal acceleration at the rim substitutes for gravity, with a despun hub for docking and microgravity work.

name: Cislunar Logistics Network
what: A permanent off-world economy requires scheduled transport, depots, salvage operations and standard interfaces across cislunar space and beyond. Today each mission is bespoke, which is the clearest sign the industrial base is still pre-network.
how: Standard docking, propellant and power interfaces let vehicles be reused across routes, with orbital transfer hubs acting as the interchange points between them.

name: In-Space Assembly and Robotic Servicing
what: Robotic assembly makes launch fairing volume the design constraint instead of the finished structure size, which is the binding limit on every large orbital system today. Servicing also extends the working life of assets that were built as expendable.
how: Free-flying robots and robotic arms join modules, replace instrument packages and refuel satellites using grappling fixtures and standard berthing mechanisms.

name: Rotating Detonation Engine
what: A rotating detonation engine burns propellant in a continuously circulating supersonic detonation wave, offering higher thermodynamic efficiency and a simpler, more compact combustor than constant-pressure rocket engines.
how: Propellant injected into an annular chamber ignites into a detonation that races continuously around the ring, consuming fresh mixture and exhausting axially; the pressure gain raises achievable specific impulse over deflagration cycles.

name: Planetary Defense Kinetic Impactor
what: Deliberately crashing a spacecraft into a hazardous near-Earth asteroid nudges its orbit years ahead of a predicted impact, the only deflection technique demonstrated end to end on a real body.
how: A high-velocity impactor transfers momentum to the asteroid; the momentum enhancement factor depends on how much ejecta the impact throws off, which must be measured by a companion observer to confirm the achieved deflection.

name: Orbital Debris Removal
what: Active removal of large defunct satellites and spent rocket bodies is the highest-leverage action against runaway collisional cascades in low Earth orbit, where a single breakup can seed thousands of trackable fragments.
how: A servicer rendezvouses with a tumbling object, captures it with a robotic arm, net or harpoon, and either deorbits it or raises it to a graveyard orbit, all within a strictly limited propellant budget.

name: Suborbital Point-to-Point Transport
what: Rocket-powered suborbital flights could cut long-haul journeys to under an hour by flying above the atmosphere for most of the trip, trading extreme acceleration and cost for speed over antipodal routes.
how: A vehicle launches onto a ballistic or depressed trajectory, coasts through near-vacuum for the majority of the flight and lands at a distant spaceport; thermal protection, acoustic loading and range safety drive the design.

name: Lunar Polar Ice Mining
what: Permanently shadowed polar craters hold water ice that can be mined for drinking water, oxygen and hydrogen-oxygen propellant, avoiding the cost of lifting volatiles out of Earth's gravity well.
how: Robotic excavators or sublimation tents either heat icy regolith in place inside the cold trap or transfer it to a sealed chamber, capturing the released water vapour for condensation and electrolysis.

name: Bioregenerative Life Support
what: Closed-loop life support uses plants, algae and microbial reactors to regenerate oxygen, water and food, cutting the resupply mass required for long-duration missions and surface habitats.
how: Crop chambers fix carbon dioxide into biomass while releasing oxygen; urine and grey water pass through biological and physicochemical processing steps, with loop mass balance tuned to the crew's metabolic load.

name: Space Domain Awareness Network
what: Ground- and space-based sensors track objects down to centimetres in orbit, providing conjunction warnings and attributing manoeuvres, the foundational layer of any sustainable orbital economy.
how: Radar and optical telescopes survey the sky for satellites and debris; catalogue data feed orbit-determination software that predicts close approaches, issues collision-avoidance alerts and detects unannounced manoeuvres.

name: Nuclear Electric Propulsion
what: A fission reactor generating electricity for high-power ion thrusters delivers far higher exhaust velocity than chemical rockets, enabling heavy cargo transfers across the inner solar system on reasonable timescales.
how: A compact reactor drives a closed Brayton or Rankine cycle that powers gridded ion or Hall-effect thrusters; low thrust applied continuously for months builds large velocity changes with a fraction of the propellant mass.

name: Solar Sail Cargo Transport
what: Large reflective sails use continuous photon pressure for propellant-free cargo delivery, well suited to slow, high-delta-v resupply of cislunar or interplanetary depots where launch mass is the binding constraint.
how: A deployed thin-film sail gains thrust from sunlight; attitude control by tilting the sail changes the thrust vector, letting the craft spiral outward over months without consuming any reaction mass.

name: Lunar Surface Power Grid
use: Shared power for habitats and processing
what: A shared electrical network linking landers, habitats and resource-processing plants at the lunar south pole avoids duplicating generation and enables the high peak loads demanded by mining and electrolysis.
how: Fission reactors or large tracking solar arrays feed a surface or shallowly buried high-voltage cable network; the architecture must survive the fourteen-day lunar night and extreme diurnal thermal cycling.

name: Gravity Tractor Asteroid Deflection
what: A spacecraft hovering near an asteroid uses its own tiny gravitational attraction, sustained over years, to tow the body slowly off a collision course without touching it.
how: The spacecraft stations itself a few hundred metres away and fires low-thrust engines to hold position; the mutual gravitational pull gradually changes the asteroid's velocity, with no risk of fragmentation.

name: Orbital Solar Power Satellite
what: Solar power satellites harvest sunlight in geostationary or low orbit and beam it to rectenna arrays on the ground, delivering continuous baseload power unaffected by weather, night or season. The end product is dispatchable electricity rather than fuel.
how: Large photovoltaic or concentrating arrays feed microwave or laser transmitters aimed at kilometre-scale rectifying antennas. Efficiency across the atmosphere is limited by beam spreading and conversion losses, which is why designs favour geostationary geometry, very large apertures and short wavelengths.

name: Nicoll-Dyson Beam
what: A Nicoll-Dyson beam is a Dyson swarm operated in phase as one giant phased array, concentrating stellar output into a beam able to accelerate lightsails across interstellar distances or act as a planetary-scale defensive system. It marks the point where a power megastructure becomes interstellar infrastructure.
how: Each swarm element carries a phase-coherent emitter, and a master clock keeps the whole array aligned so the combined aperture equals the width of the swarm orbit. Beam divergence then falls with aperture size, allowing a star's output to be focused onto a target smaller than a planet at light-year range.

name: Electromagnetic Mass Driver
what: A mass driver is a linear accelerator that launches payloads from a planetary surface or an airless moon without chemical propellant. On the Moon or an asteroid it can reach orbital velocity outright, while on Earth it can serve as a reusable first stage.
how: A long track of pulsed coils or rails accelerates a sled carrying the payload, which separates at the muzzle and continues ballistically or under its own power. Efficient pulsed power, track wear and the length required in atmosphere are the limiting factors.

name: Lunar Electromagnetic Mass Driver
use: Low-cost bulk cargo export from the Moon
what: An electromagnetic accelerator on the lunar surface could launch regolith or refined material into orbit without propellant, because the Moon's low gravity and absent atmosphere remove the two dominant costs of Earth launch. Studies treat it as a prerequisite for space-based construction at scale.
how: A linear synchronous motor along a track accelerates a carrier to lunar escape or transfer velocity; the payload is released at the track end and captured in orbit by a receiving tug.

name: Additive Construction of Planetary Habitats
use: Regolith-based shelters on the Moon and Mars
what: Contour crafting and gantry printers that build structures from local regolith or sintered simulant would eliminate the launch mass of habitat shells, which dominates settlement logistics. Earth-based analogues and NASA-funded development programmes have produced full-scale demonstration structures.
how: A gantry or robotic arm deposits a binder-activated regolith mixture in layers, or microwaves and sinters regolith directly; the printed shell is then covered with regolith for radiation shielding.

name: Kinetic Spin Launch System
use: Propellant-free launch of rugged small payloads
what: A ground-based centrifuge spins a payload to hypersonic velocity in vacuum and releases it into an ascending trajectory, eliminating first-stage propellant entirely. Payloads must tolerate thousands of g, restricting the approach to dense, robust cargo.
how: A tether in a vacuum chamber accelerates the projectile along a circular path; release occurs at a tangential point aimed at the target apogee, after which a small kick motor circularises the orbit.

name: Off-World Propellant Production
use: Return propellant, surface mobility, life support consumables
what: Producing methane and oxygen from Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide and subsurface ice removes the largest mass item from a Mars mission manifest, since return propellant is the dominant payload. Sabatier and water electrolysis are flight-proven at small scale.
how: Carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is reacted with hydrogen from electrolysed water over a nickel catalyst to form methane and water; oxygen is produced by water electrolysis and by solid-oxide electrolysis of carbon dioxide.

name: Regolith Construction and Additive Manufacturing
what: Building landing pads, shelters and roads from local material replaces the most massive payloads a mission would otherwise carry from Earth. Sintering and binder jetting have been demonstrated at small scale under vacuum and low gravity.
how: Microwave, solar or laser heating fuses regolith into solid shapes, or a binder is jetted into a regolith bed and cured, using local material as the bulk of the finished structure.

name: Asteroid Volatile Extraction
what: Water from carbonaceous asteroids is the cheapest plausible source of propellant, radiation shielding and life support for anything operating beyond low Earth orbit. No mission has yet returned volatile material at meaningful scale.
how: A captured or bagged asteroid is heated with concentrated sunlight; sublimated water is condensed, collected and electrolysed into hydrogen and oxygen.
